meta.dataStatus: Benchmarks attached from cited national surveys (Pew Research Center, Gallup, Quinnipiac, AP-NORC, YouGov, Chicago Council on Global Affairs, Annenberg APPC, BPC, PDK). Each nationalAvg is the % of the national public endorsing the right-anchor (more collective/regulated/coordinated) pole of that issue's spectrum. Demographic cells a survey does not publish are null by design — they are never estimated. Every figure traces to the cited source, field dates and question.
meta.geographicScope: United States civic attitudes with global issues included
meta.scaleNote: neutral MUST be the exact midpoint of min..max, or decisiveness becomes asymmetric.
meta.anchorNote: leftAnchorLabel/rightAnchorLabel are the poles of THIS ISSUE'S policy spectrum, not political left/right. Orientation is a scoring invariant: rightAnchorLabel is always the more collective/regulated/publicly-coordinated pole. Flipping one topic silently corrupts the composite index.
migrations: v1->v2: topic id `universal-healthcare` renamed to `healthcare-system` (identical construct and anchor orientation). Stored answers are remapped in the persisted store migration.

v1->v2: topic `trade-offshoring` has no successor in the v2 framework and is retained with topicStatus 'archived'. Historical answers keep their original meaning but no longer contribute to the composite.

v2->v3: real survey benchmarks attached (nationalAvg + demographicSplits + source) for every active topic. Demographic split cells are now nullable: `null` means the cited survey did not publish that subgroup, and is shown as 'not reported' rather than estimated. nationalAvg remains the % leaning toward the right anchor.

topics.description: How should governments balance rapid AI development and private innovation against safety requirements, accountability, transparency, and restrictions on high-risk uses?
topics.source: Quinnipiac University Poll 'The Age of Artificial Intelligence' (fielded Mar 19–23, 2026, n=1,397): 74% say the government is not doing enough to regulate the use of AI. Income cells approximate Quinnipiac's <$50K/50–100K/100–200K/$200K+ buckets. https://poll.qu.edu/poll-release?releaseid=3955

topics.topicName: AI Automation & the Future of Work
topics.description: As AI changes or replaces parts of human work, should society prioritize unrestricted automation and productivity, or require stronger worker protections, transition support, and redistribution of its gains?
topics.source: YouGov 'AI Effects on the Job Market' (fielded Mar 9–16, 2023, n=2,000): 50% say the government should regulate the use of AI in the workplace. Income cells approximate YouGov's <$50K/50–100K/$100K+ buckets. https://docs.cdn.yougov.com/0jv1wfqlmo/results_AI%20Effects%20on%20Job%20Market.pdf

topics.description: How should communities and governments manage the construction of energy- and water-intensive data centers, including their effects on electricity prices, land, jobs, water, and the power grid?
topics.source: Quinnipiac University Poll 'The Age of Artificial Intelligence' (Mar 19–23, 2026): 65% oppose the building of an AI data center in their community — the best available proxy for public/local control over data-center siting and costs. Income cells from Quinnipiac's <$50K/50–100K/100–200K/$200K+ buckets. https://poll.qu.edu/poll-release?releaseid=3955

topics.description: Should cryptocurrency and decentralized financial systems operate with broad freedom from government control, or should governments impose extensive consumer protections, financial rules, and oversight?
topics.source: YouGov (fielded Mar 6–8, 2024, n=1,092): 39% say cryptocurrency should be more regulated (36% not sure; 17% no change; 8% less). Income cells approximate YouGov's <$50K/50–100K/$100K+ buckets. https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/crosstabs_Cryptocurrency_20240319.pdf

topics.description: How should society balance personal data privacy and limits on government and corporate surveillance against security, law enforcement, and the convenience of data-driven services?
topics.source: Pew Research Center, 'How Americans View Data Privacy' (fielded May 15–21, 2023, n=5,101): 72% favor more government regulation of what companies can do with customers' personal information. Pew published only partisan splits for this item; 71% say they are very/somewhat concerned about government use of their data. https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2023/10/18/how-americans-view-data-privacy/

topics.description: Should large online platforms have broad discretion over moderation and product design, or should governments impose stronger competition rules, platform accountability, and protections for online speech and users?
topics.source: Pew Research Center, 'Americans' Views of Technology Companies' (fielded Feb 7–11, 2024, n=10,133): 51% say the government should regulate major technology companies more than it does now (16% less, 31% same). 78% say social media companies have too much power in politics. Only partisan splits published. https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/04/29/americans-views-of-technology-companies-2/

topics.description: How should the political system balance broad participation, election access, institutional checks and balances, executive power, election administration, and safeguards against abuse of power?
topics.source: Gallup (fielded Dec 1–20, 2023, n=1,013): 71% are dissatisfied with the way democracy is working in the U.S. (28% satisfied — record low). Income cells approximate Gallup's <$50K/50–100K/$100K+ buckets; Gallup's nonwhite aggregate is not broken out into Black/Hispanic/Asian/Native. https://news.gallup.com/poll/548120/record-low-satisfied-democracy-working.aspx

topics.description: What approach should the United States take toward the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including civilian protection, humanitarian assistance, military aid, Palestinian self-determination, Israeli security, settlements, accountability, and the political future of Gaza?
topics.source: Gallup (fielded Feb 2–16, 2026): 57% favor the establishment of an independent Palestinian state on the West Bank and Gaza (self-determination pole). Race limited to White vs non-white (not broken out). Compare: 41% sympathize more with the Palestinians overall. https://news.gallup.com/file/poll/702467/20260227_Israel%20Palestine.pdf

topics.description: Should the United States prioritize military deterrence and pressure against Iran, or emphasize diplomacy, negotiated limits on nuclear capabilities, sanctions relief, and reduced military involvement in the region?
topics.source: AP-NORC (fielded Mar 19–23, 2026): 59% say recent U.S. military actions against Iran have gone too far (26% about right, 13% not far enough) — the diplomacy/reduced-military-involvement pole. No demographic crosstabs published. https://apnorc.org/projects/most-say-the-united-states-recent-military-actions-against-iran-have-gone-too-far/

topics.description: What role should the United States play in the Russia-Ukraine war and European security, including military assistance, sanctions, negotiations, territorial questions, and long-term security commitments?
topics.rightAnchorLabel: Sustained Support for Ukraine & European Security
topics.source: Chicago Council on Global Affairs / Ipsos (fielded Feb 6–8, 2026): 57% support the U.S. providing military assistance to Ukraine (62% in Jul 2025). Party-only crosstabs published. 69% favor more sanctions on Russia; 65% support NATO membership for Ukraine-compatible allies' defense. https://globalaffairs.org/research/public-opinion-survey/americans-oppose-ceding-donbas-russia-amid-push-peace-deal

topics.description: How should the United States manage its relationship with China across trade, technology, Taiwan, military power, diplomacy, and economic interdependence?
topics.source: Pew Research Center Global Attitudes (Spring 2026 U.S. wave): 71% hold an unfavorable view of China (77% in 2025, 81% in 2024). Published splits are age/ideology/party only. https://alpha.pewresearch.org/pewresearch-org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2026/07/pg_2026.06.15_global-views-china-2026_report.pdf

topics.description: How much should the United States spend on defense, and when should it use military force abroad to defend allies, deter threats, protect national interests, or respond to humanitarian crises?
topics.source: Gallup (fielded Feb 2–16, 2026): 31% say U.S. national defense is not strong enough (50% about right, 17% stronger than needed); 27% favor acting alone militarily in a major crisis if allies decline. Gallup's nonwhite aggregate is not broken out into Black/Hispanic/Asian/Native. https://news.gallup.com/file/poll/702827/2026_03_05_U.S.%20Global%20Strength%20Perceptions%20Topline%20and%20Tabs.pdf

topics.description: How should the United States balance border enforcement, legal immigration, asylum, deportation, labor needs, humanitarian obligations, and pathways to legal status?
topics.source: Gallup (fielded Jun 1–15, 2026): 29% say immigration should be decreased (35% keep at present level, 31% increased; down from 55% decrease in 2024). 73% say immigration is a good thing for the country. Party-only crosstabs published. Direction cross-check: 56% favor expanding the border wall (Pew, Jun 2025). https://news.gallup.com/poll/712289/americans-support-immigration-down-strong.aspx

topics.description: How aggressively should governments act to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and protect ecosystems, including through regulation, carbon pricing, public investment, and restrictions on high-emission activities?
topics.source: Pew Research Center (fielded Oct 21–27, 2024, n=9,593): 68% favor taxing corporations based on the amount of carbon emissions they produce (61% favor requiring power plants to eliminate carbon emissions by 2040). Pew publishes party-only splits for these items. https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2024/12/09/how-americans-view-climate-change-and-policies-to-address-the-issue/

topics.description: How should governments balance affordable and reliable energy, fossil-fuel production, renewable energy, nuclear power, energy independence, and emissions reduction?
topics.source: Pew Research Center (fielded May 13–19, 2024, n=8,638): 64% say expanding wind, solar and hydrogen production should be the more important energy priority for the country (35% say oil, coal and gas). Party-by-generation splits published only. https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2024/06/27/views-on-energy-development-in-the-u-s/

topics.description: What should governments prioritize when addressing high prices and declining affordability, including monetary policy, fiscal spending, competition, price controls, and income support?
topics.source: YouGov (fielded Aug 16–19, 2024, n=1,143): 65% support capping increases on food and grocery prices (government price-control pole). Party-only splits published. Direction cross-check: 61% blame large corporations seeking maximum profits for inflation 'a lot' (YouGov). https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/50369-kamala-harris-economic-platform-resonates-across-party-lines

topics.description: How should governments address housing costs and homelessness through zoning reform, private construction, public housing, rent regulation, housing assistance, and supportive services?
topics.source: Bipartisan Policy Center / National Housing Conference via Morning Consult (2024, n=2,045): 66% say the federal government is very (36%) or somewhat (30%) responsible for ensuring families have safe, decent, affordable housing; 74% call the lack of affordable homes a significant problem. Party-only splits published. https://bipartisanpolicy.org/blog/opinions-on-housing-affordability-poll

topics.description: How should governments distribute the costs and benefits of economic growth, including taxes on income, wealth, corporations, capital gains, and inheritances, as well as social transfers?
topics.source: Pew Research Center (fielded Jan 20–26, 2026, n=8,512): 61% say the feeling that some wealthy people don't pay their fair share in federal taxes bothers them a lot (60% say this about corporations). Party-only splits published. https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/06/top-tax-frustrations-for-americans-feeling-that-some-wealthy-people-corporations-dont-pay-fair-share/

topics.description: How much power should workers and labor unions have in setting wages, working conditions, benefits, and workplace rules, and how should this be balanced against employer flexibility?
topics.source: Gallup Work & Education (fielded Aug 1–20, 2025): 68% approve of labor unions, fifth straight year in the 67–71% range. Gender (2020), race-vs-nonwhite (2019) and <$40K income (2021) cells are from earlier Gallup waves of the same question; nonwhite is not broken out. https://news.gallup.com/poll/694472/labor-union-approval-relatively-steady.aspx

topics.description: Should healthcare be guaranteed through a more publicly funded and regulated system, or should private insurance, competition, and individual choice remain the primary means of providing coverage?
topics.source: Pew Research Center (fielded Nov 17–30, 2025, n=10,357): 66% say the federal government has a responsibility to make sure all Americans have health care coverage (35% favor a single national government-run insurance program). Asian cell is English-speakers only; income cells map Pew's lower/upper terciles to <$40K/$150K+. https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/12/10/most-americans-say-government-has-a-responsibility-to-ensure-health-care-coverage/

topics.description: How should society organize and fund education, including public schools, school choice, curriculum authority, parental rights, higher education, and the role of government in educational opportunity?
topics.source: PDK Poll (fielded Mar–Apr 2024, n=1,050): 61% prefer a candidate for office who favors increased funding for the public schools (29% maintain funding, 8% cut). PDK background: ~7 in 10 Black and Hispanic adults prefer the increased-funding candidate; rural residents 51%. https://pdkpoll.org/2024-poll-results/

topics.description: How should governments balance individual freedom in matters of identity, reproduction, sexuality, religion, and personal life against collective norms, public interests, and legal restrictions?
topics.rightAnchorLabel: Greater Public Regulation & Traditional Social Norms
topics.source: Proxied by abortion attitudes (the clearest tracked personal-autonomy issue). Gallup 'Pro-Choice or Pro-Life' Demographic Table (May 1–17, 2026): 42% identify as pro-life — the restrictive pole. Gender and income cells from Gallup (income approximates <$50K/50–100K/$100K+ buckets); race cells from Pew abortion report (Apr 8–14, 2024), % who say abortion should be illegal in all or most cases. https://news.gallup.com/poll/244709/pro-choice-pro-life-2018-demographic-tables.aspx

topics.description: Should the federal government tighten or relax the rules around who can buy guns, which weapons are legal, and how firearms are carried in public?
topics.source: Pew Research Center, 'Americans and Gun Violence' (fielded Jun 5–11, 2023, n=5,115): 58% say gun laws should be stricter (26% about right, 15% less strict). Hispanic/Asian cells are English-speakers only; Pew published no income cross-tab. https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/06/28/americans-and-gun-violence/

topics.description: Should the United States pursue open trade and global supply chains, or protect domestic industry and employment through tariffs and reshoring?
